newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus standoff eases after Moscow intervenes.
newsitem.headline: Belarus standoff eases after Moscow intervenes.

text.p: A political crisis in Belarus over hardline President Alexander Lukashenko's plans to widen his powers by referendum appeared to ease on Tuesday after Russia stepped in to urge a compromise.

A senior political source in the former Soviet republic said Lukashenko expressed readiness to compromise with his opponents, possibly dropping his plans for a new constitution in exchange for parliament abandoning plans to impeach him.

The source said Lukashenko made his offer in a meeting with Valery Tikhinya, president of the Constitutional Court. "It seems that Lukashenko is ready to withdraw his constitutional draft and there will be no impeachment today. But let's see what happens tomorrow," the source said.

Political sources said, however, that the chamber, which began steps to impeach the president on Tuesday, was effectively split in two with pro-Lukashenko deputies boycotting the sessions and depriving it of a quorum.
The hint of a compromise from Lukashenko came after a day of mounting alarm among neighbouring states at the confrontation.

France expressed concern among Western states that the referendum was illegal, and there were strong hints of disquiet at Lukashenko's plans to steamroller all opposition from neighbouring Poland, Lithuania and Ukraine.
But there were signs that intervention by Russia may have been crucial in persuading Lukashenko to back off even though his parliamentary opponents were in disarray.
Russia's Interfax news agency said that after the meeting with Tikhinya, Lukashenko held a telephone conversation with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in Mosccow.
Chernomyrdin and President Boris Yeltsin, ending the Kremlin's embarrassed silence over events in Belarus, expressed alarm earlier on Tuesday at the standoff and urged a compromise solution.

"The president and the prime minister expressed alarm about rising tension in Belarus society and the hope that common sense and the art of political compromise will replace the ambitions and confrontations among politicians," a Kremlin spokesman said.

One of Lukashenko's critics, former central bank governor Stanislav Bogdankevich, told Russia's NTV television that only pressure from Moscow on Lukashenko could prevent him from increasing his powers.
Lukashenko has ignored the current constitution and rulings by the Constitutional Court in declaring that the referendum, for which voting has already started, must be binding.
It was not clear if the 42-year-old president was prepared to drop the referendum altogether or modify his position on how it should be implemented. Parliament on Tuesday began steps to impeach him.

French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt told reporters in Paris that ambassadors of France, Italy, Germany and Britain delivered a protest in Minsk. But diplomats of the four countries in the Belarussian capital said they knew nothing of any fresh protest and thought the French spokesman must have been referring to a diplomatic move some time ago.
Lukashenko has scorned Western criticism but is heavily dependent on the political winds blowing from Moscow. He and Yeltsin agreed last April to unite their countries in a "community".
Lukashenko is seeking authority to extend his term by more than two years and widen his powers over all institutions.

Prime Minister Mikhail Chigir resigned on Monday when Lukashenko refused to drop the referendum, giving the opposition a boost, but Lukashenko quickly replaced him, making deputy prime minister Sergei Ling acting premier.
On Tuesday Lukashenko turned a crowd of about 10,000 people in the small town of Borisov ecstatic by exploiting painful memories in Belarus of World War Two and the Chernobyl nuclear disaster.
"Dear people! There is a referendum on November 24. You will vote not for Lukashenko but for your lives, for the future of your children," he said.

Lukashenko sped into the small, charmless, military town of about 100,000 people 70 km (40 miles) east of Minsk in a big black Mercedes and addressed the crowd from the foot of a huge monument to Vladimir Lenin emblazoned with the words "All power to the Soviets!"

He invoked memories of World War Two, when Nazi forces overran the country between Russia and Poland, and of the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster in neighbouring Ukraine, which contaminated much of Belarus.
The crowd, mostly elderly, were overwhelmed by the appearance of their lean, angular, moustachioed president who they call "batska" in Belarussian -- or father.
